t: What a Resealable Component Organizer Box Is
title: What a Resealable Component Organizer Box Is
description: A resealable component organizer box — often called a grid box — is a shallow plastic case with fixed or adjustable compartments and a snap-shut lid, used to sort screws, washers, jumpers, standoffs, and thermal pads by type. The resealable lid keeps everything contained when the box moves, unlike open trays. For PC builders it is the long-term home for leftover screws and the staging area for multi-system jobs.

title: Fixed vs Adjustable Compartments
description: Fixed-compartment boxes have molded dividers that never shift — best for a stable screw collection you reach for weekly. Adjustable boxes use removable dividers so compartments resize around odd items like WiFi antennas or long standoffs. For PC work, adjustable wins: today's build needs big compartments for PSU screws, tomorrow's needs tiny ones for M.2 hardware, and the box reconfigures in seconds.

demo.program:
print("Fixed: molded dividers, stable, best for a permanent screw library")
print("Adjustable: removable dividers, reconfigures per build")
print("PC verdict: adjustable - compartment needs change every build.")
print("Tip: keep 2-3 divider layouts photographed for repeat jobs.")

title: Standard Sizes and Compartment Counts
description: Common grid boxes run from pocket-size 6-compartment cases up to 36-compartment bench boxes around 11 by 7 inches. Deep boxes (2-inch compartments) hold standoffs and thumbscrews standing up; shallow boxes suit washers and jumpers. A two-box system covers most builders: one 18-compartment box for active build hardware, one 36-compartment box as the permanent screw library.

demo.program:
boxes = [("pocket 6-ct", "travel kit"), ("bench 18-ct", "active build staging"),
         ("library 36-ct", "permanent screw collection")]
for name, use in boxes:
    print(f"  {name:<14} -> {use}")
print("Two-box system: 18-ct active + 36-ct library covers most builders.")

t: The Screw Library: Building a Permanent Sorted Collection
title: The Screw Library: Building a Permanent Sorted Collection
description: Every leftover screw from every build goes into the library box, sorted by type into labeled compartments — and after a few builds you stop buying screw assortments because the library covers it. Sort by thread and length (M3x5, M3x8, #6-32x1/4), not by where the screw came from. A screw gauge card in the lid identifies mystery screws in seconds. The library is the highest-return organizer a builder owns.

t: Labeling Compartments So the System Survives Time
title: Labeling Compartments So the System Survives Time
description: An unlabeled grid box becomes a mystery box within a month. Label each compartment with thread, length, and head type using a label maker or masking tape and marker — 'M3x5 P2' beats 'small screws'. Put the label on the lid above each compartment, not inside it, so labels stay readable when compartments are full. Re-label when a compartment's contents change; stale labels are worse than none.

demo.program:
labels = ["M3x5 P2", "M3x8 P2", "#6-32x1/4", "M2x3", "standoff M3", "jumper"]
print("Label format: thread x length + drive (P2/T10/hex)")
for l in labels:
    print(f"  [{l}]")
print("Labels on the LID above compartments, re-labeled when contents change.")

t: Use Case: Staging a Full Build From the Library
title: Use Case: Staging a Full Build From the Library
description: Before a build, pull the full screw set from the library into the active box: nine standoffs, nine board screws, PSU screws, drive screws, fan screws — each in its own compartment, counted. The build then runs without a single trip to the parts drawer. Count compartments, not piles: an empty compartment at the end means its screws all went in, a full one means you missed them.

t: Use Case: Multi-System and Server Screw Management
title: Use Case: Multi-System and Server Screw Management
description: Server and multi-system jobs multiply screw counts past what a tray can hold — a 4-node build can involve 200 screws. The grid box stages one compartment per node per screw type, so node 3's board screws never mix with node 1's. Lid-closed transport between bench and rack keeps sets intact. For rack work, photograph each loaded box before leaving the bench.

t: Grid Box vs Parts Tray vs Bins: When Each Wins
title: Grid Box vs Parts Tray vs Bins: When Each Wins
description: Grid boxes win for sorted storage and transport — lids keep sets intact. Parts trays win for active handling — open, magnetic, one-hand access. Parts bins win for bulky items like fans and brackets that do not fit compartments. The working system uses all three: bins for bulk, grid box for sorted staging and storage, tray for the screws in your hand right now.

print("tray     : active handling (open, magnetic, one-hand)")
print("bins     : bulky items (fans, brackets, manuals)")
print("System: bins -> grid box -> tray, bulk to hand in three stages.")

t: Keeping Tiny Parts From Migrating Between Compartments
title: Keeping Tiny Parts From Migrating Between Compartments
description: Cheap boxes let M.2 screws hop compartments when the lid flexes. Fix it three ways: buy boxes with dividers that reach the lid (no gap to hop), keep the box flat in transport, and put the tiniest hardware in small zip bags inside compartments. The bag-in-compartment trick also lets you pull one screw type out as a unit for a field repair without dumping the box.

demo.program:
print("Anti-migration rules:")
print("  1. dividers must reach the lid (no hop gap)")
print("  2. transport flat, lid latched")
print("  3. tiniest hardware in zip bags INSIDE compartments")
print("Bonus: bag = one screw type lifts out as a unit for field work.")

title: Cleaning and Maintaining Grid Boxes
description: Dump each compartment yearly, wipe the box with a damp cloth, and audit: mystery screws get gauged and labeled or discarded, duplicates consolidate, and empty compartments get relabeled to current needs. Check divider fit — warped dividers let parts migrate and should be replaced. A ten-minute annual audit keeps the library trustworthy; a neglected box becomes a junk drawer with a lid.

demo.program:

print("  - dump, wipe with damp cloth")
print("  - gauge mystery screws: label or discard")
print("  - consolidate duplicates, relabel empties")
print("  - replace warped dividers (migration risk)")

title: Stackable Systems and Drawer Integration
description: Bench boxes from one product family stack and latch together, so the active box rides on the library box as a single unit. Shallow boxes slide into desk drawers as drawer organizers; deep boxes live on shelves. Standardize on one footprint so every box stacks with every other — mixed brands never nest and waste the space they were meant to save.

print("  - same brand/family: stacks latch into one unit")
print("  - shallow boxes: desk drawer organizers")
print("  - deep boxes: shelf storage")
print("Mixed brands never nest: standardization IS the space saving.")

t: Buying Guide: Latches, Hinges, and Divider Quality
title: Buying Guide: Latches, Hinges, and Divider Quality
description: Check the latch first — it must snap positively and survive drops; weak latches pop open in bags. Hinges should be living-hinge polypropylene or pinned, not thin scored plastic that cracks in a year. Dividers must fit tight with no hop gap. Clear lids beat opaque: you see contents without opening. Expect 8 to 25 dollars; the 3-dollar boxes fail at the latch within months.

demo.program:
checks = [("latch snaps positive, survives drop test", True),
          ("hinge: living-hinge or pinned", True),
          ("dividers tight, no hop gap", True),
          ("clear lid (see contents closed)", True)]
for c, _ in checks:
    print(f"  PASS required: {c}")
print("Price: $8-25. The $3 box fails at the latch within months.")

t: Advanced: Kanban Restocking for the Screw Library
title: Advanced: Kanban Restocking for the Screw Library
description: High-volume builders run the library like inventory: each compartment gets a minimum count, and when a compartment drops below it, that screw type goes on the buy list. A card in the lid lists minimums; a glance shows what to order. This kanban trick means the library never runs dry mid-build — the system reorders itself before a shortage stops work.

title: Pro Technique: The Photographed Load-Out
description: Before any off-bench job, photograph the loaded grid box with the lid open — every compartment visible. The photo is the packing list, the reassembly reference, and the loss detector: anything missing at the end shows as a wrong compartment in the photo. Combined with the screw tray's count gate, the photographed load-out closes the last gap in hardware accountability.

print("  2. photograph from directly above")
print("  3. photo = packing list + reassembly ref + loss detector")
print("End of job: compare box to photo; every compartment must match.")
